title: Molybdenum in Plants: What It Does and When Your Crop Needs It
metaTitle: Molybdenum in Plants: Role, Signs and When It Matters
metaDescription: Molybdenum in plants turns nitrate into protein and feeds legume nodules. See which crops need it, why acid soils run short, and how little it takes.
excerpt: Molybdenum in plants is the smallest need of all, often less than a hundred grams per hectare, yet without it a crop cannot use the nitrate it takes up, and a legume cannot fix nitrogen. Acid soils run short most often. Here is what it does, which crops need it most, and how little it takes to fix.

heroImage.alt: Young corn plant on acid soil with pale, dying older leaves: molybdenum in plants running short
heroImage.credit: Alandmanson, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Molybdenum is part of the enzyme that turns nitrate, the form most nitrogen reaches the roots in, into a form the plant can build protein with. A plant short of it piles up nitrate and still looks hungry for nitrogen.

In legumes like mungbean, peanut, sitaw and soybean, molybdenum is part of the enzyme in the root nodules that fixes nitrogen from the air. So a legume short of molybdenum stays pale and yields little, however well its nodules form.
A helper, the smallest need of all

Molybdenum is a helper. It sits inside two or three enzymes and works without being used up, so a crop needs less of it than of any other nutrient.

That tiny need is why a seed treatment or a single light spray is usually enough for a whole season.

blocks.caption: Molybdenum in short
rows: The old and middle leaves, pale like nitrogen

blocks.text:
Molybdenum moves fairly well inside the plant, and because it works through nitrogen, its shortage looks like nitrogen shortage: pale older leaves, slow growth and in legumes, poor nodules. Cabbage and cauliflower get narrow, ragged leaves called whiptail.

See [molybdenum deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/molybdenum-deficiency) for the signs crop by crop.
When molybdenum in plants is most critical

Molybdenum matters most for legumes while their nodules form and work, and for cabbage, cauliflower and other crucifers in their early growth. Palay needs almost none.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing molybdenum in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

blocks.text: What keeps molybdenum from the crop

Unlike most trace nutrients, molybdenum becomes harder to take up as the soil turns more acid. So strongly acid soils run short most often, and liming them often fixes the shortage by itself.

Heavy sulfate fertilizer can also compete with it at the roots.

Sodium or ammonium molybdate, used as a seed coating for legumes or a weak spray, supplies enough for the season. Liming acid soil frees what is already there. See [fertilizer for vegetables](/blog/fertilizer-for-vegetables-philippines) for the crops that need it most.

items: Sodium molybdate or ammonium molybdate: as a seed coating or a weak spray.
Lime on acid soil: frees the molybdenum the soil holds.

blocks.title: A few grams is plenty
blocks.text: Molybdenum is needed in grams per hectare. Much more builds up in forage and can harm cattle that eat it, so stay at the label rate.

blocks.title: Plan molybdenum for your legumes and crucifers
blocks.text: Put your fertilizers on your crop's calendar in anee.io and the [Coverage Planner](/features/residual-effect-calendar) shows, day by day, whether molybdenum reaches the stages that need it, and where it runs out. Free to start.
blocks.label: Start free

items.a: Legumes, which need it to fix nitrogen, and cabbage, cauliflower and other crucifers. Palay and mais need almost none.

items.q: Why does acid soil lack molybdenum?
items.a: In acid soil molybdenum binds tightly and the roots cannot take it. Liming frees it.
A molybdenum shortage in cauliflower and cabbage that makes the leaves narrow and ragged.

items.q: How much molybdenum does a crop need?
items.a: Very little, often less than a hundred grams per hectare, so a seed coating or one light spray is usually enough.
